section.title: A better way to detect PMTU increases
section.content: Section 6.3 suggests periodically increasing the PTMU estimate to the first-hop MTU, but this can cause many dropped datagrams if rediscovered often. A superior approach is to increase the PMTU estimate incrementally to the next-highest value in the plateau table (or the actual first-hop MTU). If the new estimate fails, only one round-trip time (RTT) is wasted before correcting upward again. After each failure, progressively larger increases are attempted over longer intervals until a valid MTU is found.
section.recommendation: Use short timeouts after failed attempts and progressively longer timeouts for higher estimates to minimize disruption.

security_considerations.summary: This mechanism enables two denial-of-service attacks via forged Datagram Too Big messages indicating incorrect PMTUs. The first attack can slow data flow by suggesting a much lower maximum MTU than reality; the second may temporarily block traffic until routers send corrective messages. However, hosts should never raise their PTMU estimate based solely on such messages and are not vulnerable if they ignore them.
recommendations: Do not set PMTU estimates below the minimum possible
Limit timeouts after errors (e.g., Datagram Too Big) to 10 minutes; reduce further for larger MTUs
Gradually increase estimated MTU upon successful transmissions

implementation_notes.guidance: The table should not be overly dense, as frequent searches are costly. Allow client code to update values transparently without source code changes (e.g., via new ioctl commands). For small powers of 2 plus 40 (for IP/TCP headers), add entries where no similar value exists for clarity.
implementation_notes.arbitrary_values: Small increments near large powers are preferable; avoid excessively high or low values to ensure predictable table lookups.
